metadata.title: English Grammar Content
metadata.regional_usage: British and American variants retained where appropriate.
metadata.purpose: Reusable grammar explanations, examples, exercises, and embedded editorial answers.

reading_contract.primary_content: sections -> lessons -> teaching_block_ids and activities -> content_block_ids; resolve IDs in source_blocks recursively.
reading_contract.paragraph_text: text is the edited text for presentation; source_text is provenance and must not also be rendered.
reading_contract.tables: Retain row/cell order, paragraph boundaries, column spans, and vertical merges.
reading_contract.formatting: Offsets use zero-based Unicode code points, end exclusive. Source formatting is retained separately. Edited formatting is mapped only where the source text still matches.
reading_contract.responses: Each response_field binds exactly one answer-key part. replace_span replaces its target range; after_prompt presents a separate complete response; annotate_span marks its target; read_only_example renders the supplied example without an input. Offsets are Unicode code points. Never fill worked-example underscore padding. For after_prompt fields, provide a distinct response control or writing area for each editable field. Labels describe the requested output.
reading_contract.worked_examples: Render worked_example items and their supplied solution content as read-only. Response fields with editable=false are not unanswered quiz inputs; underscore padding in such items must not produce new questions.
reading_contract.answer_key: Keys remain exclusively in answer_key.entries. Resolve item.answer_key_id and each part.response_field_id. Per-item response_mode and instruction_block_id are authoritative. Alternatives are not exhaustive; automatic grading remains disabled.
reading_contract.scope: Only instructional content is included. Technical source locations and original instructional wording support traceability; they are not presentation content.

source_blocks.source_text: Present and Past

source_blocks.text: Present Continuous (I’m doing)
source_blocks.source_text: Present Continuous (I’m doing)

source_blocks.text: Construction
source_blocks.source_text: Construction

source_blocks.text: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing
source_blocks.source_text: Subject + to be (present tense) + verb (present participle)

source_blocks.text: I am / he, she, it is / we, you, they are + verb-ing
source_blocks.source_text: I’m / he’s / she’s / it’s / we’re / you’re / they’re + verb + -ing

blocks.text: affirmative
I’m swimming.
She’s driving.
They’re playing.
negative
I’m not shouting.
He isn’t looking.
We’re not sleeping.
question
Are you studying?
Is it working?
Are you writing?

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use the present continuous for actions happening now or around the present time.
source_blocks.source_text: For things that we are doing at the moment we are speaking.  Things happening now, right this second.

source_blocks.text: The teacher is talking.
source_blocks.source_text: The teacher is talking.

source_blocks.text: Dave is speaking with Mary.
source_blocks.source_text: Dave is speaking with Mary.

source_blocks.text: For things happening in the world during this time, but not permanently.
source_blocks.source_text: For things happening in the world during this time, but not permanently.

source_blocks.text: Schools are improving.
source_blocks.source_text: Schools are improving.

source_blocks.text: The world is changing.
source_blocks.source_text: The world is changing.

source_blocks.text: Use the present continuous for future arrangements, usually with a stated or understood future time.
source_blocks.source_text: For actions happening in the future.

source_blocks.text: I am flying to Miami next week.
source_blocks.source_text: I am flying to Miami next week.

source_blocks.text: I’m having a party on my birthday.
source_blocks.source_text: I’m having a party on my birthday.

source_blocks.text: Complete the exercise with the present continuous form of the verb in parentheses. Don’t forget the auxiliary verb! The first one is done for you.
source_blocks.source_text: Complete the exercise with the present continuous form of the verb in parentheses.  Don’t forget the auxiliary verb!  The first one is done for you.

source_blocks.text: Please turn down the music. I _ __ am trying _____ _ (try) to study.
source_blocks.source_text: Please turn down the music. I ___am trying______  (try) to study.

source_blocks.text: Why don’t we play outside? It ________________________ (not rain) anymore.
source_blocks.source_text: Why don’t we play outside?. It ________________________  (not rain) anymore.

source_blocks.text: Can you turn off the computer? I ________________________ (not use) it.
source_blocks.source_text: Can you turn off the computer?. I ________________________  (not listen) it.

source_blocks.text: My sister called from Beijing. She ________________________ (have) lots of fun!
source_blocks.source_text: My sister called from Beijing.  She ________________________  (have) lots of fun!

source_blocks.text: I ________________________ (get) frustrated. I need a break.
source_blocks.source_text: I ________________________ (get) frustrated. I need a break.

source_blocks.text: Complete the exercise with the present continuous form of the verb in parentheses. Don’t forget the auxiliary verb!
source_blocks.source_text: Complete the exercise with the present continuous form of the verb in parentheses.  Don’t forget the auxiliary verb!

source_blocks.text: ___________ they _ __________ over for lunch? (come)
source_blocks.source_text: ___________ they ___________over for lunch? (come)

source_blocks.text: The dog ______________________________ on our sofa. (not sleep)
source_blocks.source_text: The dog ______________________________ on our sofa. (not sleep)

source_blocks.text: I ______________________________ breakfast at the moment.	(have)
source_blocks.source_text: I ______________________________ breakfast at the moment.	(have)

source_blocks.text: I _____________________________ on vacation until January. (not go)
source_blocks.source_text: I _____________________________ on vacation until January. (not go)

source_blocks.text: We ______________________________ dinner at a French restaurant tonight. (have).
source_blocks.source_text: We ______________________________ dinner at a French restaurant tonight. (have).

source_blocks.text: Jamie ______________________________ her birthday today. (celebrate)
source_blocks.source_text: Jamie______________________________her birthday today. (celebrate)

source_blocks.text: They ______________________________ an online bookstore. (browse)
source_blocks.source_text: They ______________________________ an online bookstore. (browse)

source_blocks.text: Present Simple (I do)
source_blocks.source_text: Present Simple (I do)

source_blocks.text: Construction
source_blocks.source_text: Construction

source_blocks.text: Affirmative: subject + base verb (add -s or -es for he/she/it). With be, use am/is/are.
source_blocks.source_text: Affirmative	: Subject + verb in present tense + predicate

source_blocks.text: Negative: subject + do/does not + base verb. Question: do/does + subject + base verb? With be, add not or invert am/is/are and the subject.
source_blocks.source_text:
Negative	: Subject + verb in present tense, negative form + predicate
Question	: Verb in present tense + subject + predicate

blocks.text: affirmative
I am a student.
He paints houses.
She helps children learn to walk.
blocks.source_text: She helps children learn to walk.

blocks.text: negative
I am not a professor
It doesn’t work.
They don’t like to study.
question
Are you ready?
Does it turn on?
Does he make a lot of money?
blocks.source_text: Does he make a lot of money?

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use the present simple for general truths and facts that are true at the time of speaking.
source_blocks.source_text: For statements of fact that never change.

source_blocks.text: My name is Rena.
source_blocks.source_text: My name is Rena.

source_blocks.text: The earth is not the center of the universe.
source_blocks.source_text: The earth is not the center of the universe.

source_blocks.text: For conditions that are true in repeated time.
source_blocks.source_text: For conditions that are true in repeated time.

source_blocks.text: We take a shower every morning.
source_blocks.source_text: We take a shower every morning.

source_blocks.text: Dad doesn’t work weekends.
source_blocks.source_text: Dad doesn’t work weekends.

source_blocks.source_text: I _________ computer games. (play)

source_blocks.source_text: She _____________ to the USA every year. (travel)

source_blocks.source_text: They ____________ swimming. (love)

source_blocks.source_text: Our dog __________ all day. (sleep)

source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Stative verbs often describe thoughts, feelings, possession, or perception and usually take a simple form: know, believe, understand, belong, want, need, and prefer. Some verbs also have action meanings that allow a continuous form; compare I think you are right with I am thinking about the problem.
source_blocks.source_text: There are some action words that are not usually used in present continuous form.  These include  like, love, hate, want, need, prefer, know, realize, suppose, mean, understand, believe, remembers, belong, fit, contain, consist, seem, see, hear, and smell.  If presently done, use present form only.

source_blocks.text: Use be + being + adjective for temporary behavior. This does not have the same meaning as a general description with be.
source_blocks.source_text: Use being to restate something which describes the subject.

source_blocks.source_text: The kids are rowdy = The kids are being rowdy.

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use will for decisions made as you speak, offers, promises, and predictions. Use be going to for prior intentions and predictions based on present evidence. Some contexts allow either form with a difference in emphasis.
source_blocks.source_text: Use will for actions that are to be carried out at the time of speaking.  Use going to when it is connected to now.

source_blocks.text: Use when when you treat a future event as expected to occur. Use if to make the result conditional on whether an event occurs. These choices express the speaker’s perspective, not a guarantee.

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use can for one’s ability to do something. Negative form is cannot (can’t). Past tense is could.
source_blocks.source_text: Use can for one’s ability to do something.  Negative form is cannot (can’t).  Past tense is could.

source_blocks.text: Use be able to where a form of can is unavailable, for example will be able to or have been able to. Could also expresses possibility and politeness, not only past ability.
source_blocks.source_text: Use be able to if can cannot be used (since can has only two forms: present (can) and past (could).

source_blocks.text: For a particular successful action in the past, usually use was/were able to or managed to. Could is common for general past ability and with perception or mental-process verbs; couldn’t can describe a particular failure.
source_blocks.source_text: Use was able to or managed to for specific actions done in the past.

source_blocks.source_text: For things that are being imagined

source_blocks.text: I would love to see the North Pole one day.

source_blocks.text: Use would have + past participle for an imagined past result, often in a conditional sentence.
source_blocks.source_text: Use would have done for actions in the past.

source_blocks.text: She would have loved it if she had seen this view.
source_blocks.source_text: She would have loved it if she saw this view.

source_blocks.text: Mary would have come earlier if she had known Mr. Gomez had already left.
source_blocks.source_text: Mary would have come earlier if she knew Mr. Gomez had already left.

source_blocks.text: Negative form is would not (wouldn’t).
source_blocks.source_text: Negative form is would not (wouldn’t).

source_blocks.text: Fritz tried to stop him but she wouldn’t listen to him.
source_blocks.source_text: Fritz tried to stop him but she wouldn’t listen to him.

source_blocks.text: I pushed the slab really hard but it wouldn’t move.
source_blocks.source_text: I pushed the slab really hard but it wouldn’t move.

source_blocks.text: Sometimes, would is used as past tense for will/won’t.
source_blocks.source_text: Sometimes, would is used as past tense for will/won’t.

source_blocks.text: Henry said that he would vote for you if you ran for office.
source_blocks.source_text: Henry said that he would vote for you if you ran for office.

source_blocks.text: Marty told me that he wouldn’t be able to pick you up.
source_blocks.source_text: Marty told me that he wouldn’t be able to pick you up.

source_blocks.text: One can also use would to speak of something done regularly in the past.
source_blocks.source_text: One can also use would to speak of something done regularly in the past.

source_blocks.text: Construction and Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Construction and Usage

source_blocks.text: Use if + present simple for a real or possible condition; the result clause often uses will + base verb.
source_blocks.source_text: Use if I do for something is most likely to happen.

source_blocks.text: If I do my best, I’ll succeed.
source_blocks.source_text: If I do my best, I’ll succeed.

source_blocks.text: If Melissa sees this, she’ll be so happy.
source_blocks.source_text: If Melissa sees this, she’ll be so happy.

source_blocks.text: Use If I did for things that are just being imagined.

source_blocks.source_text: If I went to the party, I wouldn’t be feeling better.

source_blocks.text: In ordinary future and hypothetical conditionals, put will/would in the result clause rather than the if-clause. Other uses, such as willingness in If you would help, are possible.
source_blocks.source_text: If…would or If…wouldn’t can be used but not in the if- part.

source_blocks.text: Construction

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use if + past for imagining situations like these:
source_blocks.source_text: Use if + past for imagining situations like these:

source_blocks.text: Use wish + past form for a present situation you would like to be different.

source_blocks.text: Were is used with all subjects in formal hypothetical clauses, as in If I were you. Was is also common with I/he/she/it in informal usage.

source_blocks.text: If I were there, I wouldn’t be here. Informally, was can replace were.

source_blocks.text: If Tim were here, this wouldn’t happen. If Tim was here is also common informally.
source_blocks.source_text: If Time were here, this wouldn’t happen or If Tim was here, this wouldn’t happen.

source_blocks.text: Construction
source_blocks.source_text: Construction

source_blocks.source_text: I (subject) wish(es) + had + past participle of the verb

source_blocks.text: Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Usage

source_blocks.text: Use if + past perfect for an unreal past condition. The result commonly uses would/could/might have + past participle.
source_blocks.source_text: Use if + had to talk about the past.

source_blocks.text: If I had talked to you, I wouldn’t have made that decision.
source_blocks.source_text: If I had talked to you, I wouldn’t have made that decision.

source_blocks.text: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
source_blocks.source_text: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.

source_blocks.text: Use wish + past perfect to express regret about a past situation or action.
source_blocks.source_text: Use I wish I had to wish for something that had happened

source_blocks.text: I wish I had talked to you before making that decision.
source_blocks.source_text: I wish I had talked to you before making that decision.

source_blocks.text: I wish I had seen you before you left.
source_blocks.source_text: I wish I had seen you before you left.

source_blocks.text: In ordinary third conditionals, use had + past participle in the if-clause and would have + past participle in the result clause.
source_blocks.source_text: Never use would in the if-part.

source_blocks.text: The –ing form of verbs usually follow the following: enjoy, suggest, mind, stop, postpone, admit, avoid, imagine, finish, consider, deny, risk, and fancy.

source_blocks.text: The –ing form of verbs also follow after keep/keep on, give up, put off, or go on/carry on.

source_blocks.text: Begin, start, and continue can often be followed by either a to-infinitive or an -ing form. This is not the same as verb + object + to-infinitive.
source_blocks.source_text: With these words, you can use either verb + ing format or verb + object + to: begin, bother, start, intend, or continue.

source_blocks.text: After a continuous form of begin or start, a to-infinitive is usually more natural: It is beginning to rain. There is no general ban on two -ing forms: I am enjoying learning is grammatical.
source_blocks.source_text: One never doubles up on –ing format.  It’s wrong to say: I’m intending staying.

source_blocks.text: Relative clauses modify a noun or noun phrase, identifying or adding information about people, things, places, or times. They may begin with who, whom, whose, which, that, where, or when. The two main types are defining and non-defining.
source_blocks.source_text: Relative clauses are short phrases beginning with words called relative pronouns (who/which/that) that describe or define people, things, places, possessions and time. There are two types: defining and non-defining.

source_blocks.text: A defining relative clause identifies exactly which person, thing, or place we mean.

source_blocks.text: Construction and Usage
source_blocks.source_text: Construction and Usage

source_blocks.text: These words modify degree, but their strength depends on context, dialect, and the adjective. Fairly often suggests a moderate degree; pretty is informal.
source_blocks.source_text: They all have very similar meaning--- less than very but more than a little.

source_blocks.text: Pretty is used mostly in spoken English because it’s informal.
source_blocks.source_text: Pretty is used mostly in spoken English because it’s informal.

source_blocks.text: With gradable adjectives, quite often means moderately, especially in British English. With some non-gradable adjectives it can mean completely. Note the word order in quite a good result and quite a lot.
source_blocks.source_text: Quite is followed by a/an + adjective, noun or we can say quite a lot (of) as well. Quite is used with verbs especially like and enjoy. It also means completely-quite sure. It can be used with verbs to have the same meaning.

source_blocks.text: Rather often suggests surprise, an unexpected degree, or a negative judgment, but it can also occur in positive descriptions.

source_blocks.text: Fairly generally means moderately. It can imply a qualified assessment, but does not always mean that something is unsatisfactory.

source_blocks.text: Many frequency adverbs normally come before a main lexical verb but after be: She often visits; she is often late. Adverb position also depends on meaning and emphasis.

source_blocks.text: In many multi-verb constructions, frequency adverbs come after the first auxiliary or modal: She has often visited; she can usually help.

source_blocks.text: The basic difference between in and at is that we use in when we think about the building itself, or if we use it with cities, villages.
